claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 is a high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical heterostructure.
The initial microstructure can be characterized by grain-boundary chemistry and short-range-order distribution using APT and complementary imaging.
A hybrid framework will couple detailed molecular-dynamics simulations with machine-learning algorithms.
The framework will use experimentally calibrated APT-derived short-range-order descriptors and explicitly modeled hierarchical-interface characteristics as input features.
Grain-boundary chemistry, local disordered zones, and the spatial distribution and intensity of short-range-order clusters are the mediating microstructural parameters.
Machine learning can identify and prioritize heterostructure descriptors from molecular-dynamics outputs and experimentally measured short-range-order metrics.
Using the selected descriptors to recalibrate simulation parameters will reduce computational demand while preserving or improving predictive fidelity.
Direct experimental short-range-order measurements will mitigate machine-learning overfitting.
Integrating short-range-order measurements with ML-augmented molecular dynamics will bridge atomic-scale phenomena and macroscopic mechanical properties.
The integrated framework will predict Young's modulus within ±5% of independent measurements.
The integrated framework will predict yield strength within ±5% of independent measurements.
The integrated framework will predict fracture-related behavior within ±5% of independent measurements.
The integrated framework will achieve predictive accuracy greater than 90%.
The integrated framework will reduce simulation time by approximately 40–50% relative to established full-scale simulations.
Traditional full-scale molecular-dynamics simulations and conventional micromechanical models generally require longer computation times and iterative calibration.
The approach may fail if APT cannot reliably quantify short-range order over representative volumes.
The approach may fail if the machine-learning model does not robustly represent complex multiscale heterostructural features.
A scale mismatch between molecular-dynamics outputs and experimental conditions may limit model transferability.
The hypothesis is falsified if any predicted mechanical property differs from an independent experimental measurement by more than ±5%.
The hypothesis is also considered falsified if high-throughput APT does not consistently reveal short-range-order features correlated with the predicted property changes.
